statement: A band of 7 players chooses 3 of them to play a trio, and then one of those 3 is chosen to play the solo. In how many ways can this be done?

choices.misconception: I counted the ways to choose the trio and forgot to choose who plays the solo.
I counted ordered choices, $7 \times 6 \times 5$, as if all three players had different roles.
I chose the soloist and then chose the other two from all 7 players again, including the soloist.
I used $7 \times 7 \times 7$, which allows the same player to be chosen more than once.

hints: Choose the soloist first, then the other two.
Only one of the three has a special role. Either choose the soloist and then a pair from the rest, or choose the trio and then pick its soloist. Both orders must agree.
Soloist: 7 ways. The other two from the remaining 6: $\binom{6}{2} = 15$ ways.

solutions.reliable: Choose the soloist in 7 ways, then the other two members from the remaining 6 players in $\binom{6}{2} = 15$ ways. That gives $7 \times 15 = 105$. Check another way: choose the trio in $\binom{7}{3} = 35$ ways, then its soloist in 3 ways, giving $35 \times 3 = 105$. The transferable idea: when a selection has one special role, choose that role and the plain group separately.
solutions.elegant: Of the $7 \times 6 \times 5 = 210$ ordered choices, each outcome appears twice, because the two non-soloists can be listed in either order. So there are $210 / 2 = 105$.

whyOnTest: A selection with one special member checks whether a student separates order that matters from order that does not.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
